extracted.intended_audience: advertising/marketing professionals, brand/PR/legal teams, and readers interested in advertising regulation and greenwashing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for judging whether environmental (green) claims in advertising are misleading or acceptable under ASA practice — including how consumers will interpret taglines/imagery, what qualification/substantiation is required, and how aspirational targets and offsets are treated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity / ambiguity of the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim is clear or ambiguous — e.g., the ASA considered that, 'in isolation, the claim was ambiguous and not clearly linked to climate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An environmental-sounding tagline must be sufficiently clear about what it means; vague or ambiguous statements that could be read in an environmental way can be misleading if not clarified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable consumer interpretation (environmental reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether consumers would interpret the claim as an environmental reference — the ASA considered the claim 'Protecting its Future' was likely to be interpreted by consumers as referring to how Lufthansa’s approach was protecting the future of the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess ads from the perspective of likely consumer understanding; imagery and wording that together connote environmental protection will be read that way unless clearly disclaimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for qualification of absolute claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute-sounding claims must be qualified with contextual/temporal information — the ASA noted 'the claim “Protecting its Future” is not qualified with this information.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an advertiser's statement refers to future targets, specific initiatives, or partial measures, the ad should include qualifying information so consumers don't assume an absolute current status (e.g., 'we aim to be carbon neutral by 2050' vs 'we are protecting the planet now').

rubrics_metrics.name: Present actions versus future aspirations
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between current, demonstrable mitigations and long-term aspirations — the ASA noted many initiatives/targets 'were targeted to deliver results only years or decades into the future' and therefore did not substantiate an immediate absolute environmental claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims implying current environmental protection cannot be supported solely by distant or aspirational targets; advertisers should not present future commitments as evidence of present-state outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantiation: availability of initiatives/technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims asserting absolute environmental benefits must be supportable by existing initiatives or commercially viable technologies — the ASA said 'there were currently no environmental initiatives or commercially viable technologies in the aviation industry that would substantiate the absolute green claim “Protecting its Future”.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before making absolute environmental claims, confirm that demonstrable, industry-available measures substantiate them; lack of viable tech or initiatives undermines absolute claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Net impact implication (no-harm implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether a claim leads consumers to believe the advertiser's net environmental impact is not harmful — ASA considered consumers would interpret 'Protecting its Future' to mean Lufthansa had 'already taken significant mitigating steps to ensure that the net environmental impact of their business was not harmful.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers must avoid wording that implies their operations cause no environmental harm unless they can robustly substantiate that conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual influence of imagery and text
rubrics_metrics.description: How imagery together with wording shapes interpretation — the Lufthansa poster used an image of a plane with the earth as the underside plus the tagline, which the ASA judged would link the claim to environmental protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the combined effect of visuals and copy; imagery that evokes the planet/climate increases the likelihood that text will be read as an environmental claim and so requires appropriate qualification/substantiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutiny of 'net zero' and 'carbon neutral' claims (offset-based claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ASA is tightening regulation around brands making 'net zero' and 'carbon neutral' claims, 'particularly where those claims are based on offset emissions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims relying on offsets face heightened scrutiny; advertisers should be careful to explain the role, scale and robustness of offsets, and not to rely on offsets alone to justify absolute environmental claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: General prohibition on misleading impression about environmental impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Ads must not give a misleading impression of the advertiser’s environmental impact — the ASA 'challenged whether the ad gave a misleading impression of the advertiser’s environmental impact.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims for potential to mislead about scale, timing, or completeness of environmental actions; if the overall impression overstates environmental performance, the ad may be banned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedent and sectoral risk (aviation under increased scrutiny)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aviation firms have recently faced bans, investigations and litigation for greenwashing (examples: EasyJet investigation, KLM lawsuit), indicating greater regulatory attention to the sector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers in sectors under scrutiny should apply extra caution in environmental communications, ensuring stronger substantiation and clearer qualifications to avoid enforcement or litigation.
